catalog_quote: Gussenhoven 2000 (Roermond): "Within the word, two types of restriction conspire to confine the tonal contrast to certain locations. Firstly, the contrast is restricted to the syllable with main stress. The dialect of Roermond has the same stress system as standard Dutch. Main stress falls on either of the rightmost two syllables of the word if the penult is closed, and on one of the last three rightmost syllables if the penult is open. A final syllable without main word stress can be strong, i.e. form a foot. Secondly, the contrast is restricted to syllables with two sonorant moras. Thus, the syllable rime must contain a long vowel, a diphthong, or a lax vowel followed by a sonorant consonant ... in order for the contrast to exist. As a result, words whose main-stressed syllable contains only a single sonorant mora have neither Accent I nor Accent II." Peters 2006 (Hasselt): "Stress lo…

Samenstellingen hebben overigens (minstens) twee van zulke plaatsen, omdat elk samenstellend woord onafhankelijk een woordaccent bijdraagt. 3. Zinsaccenten. Onafhankelijk van het tooncontrast worden woorden geaccentueerd in de zin, op dezelfde manier als in het Standaardduits en Standaardnederlands.” p. 105: “Hermans (1994) noemt woorden met de klemtoon op de voorvoorlaatste en een secundaire klemtoon op de laatste lettergreep, zoals 1alge1bra, 1domi1nee, die in het Maasbrachts alleen Accent 2 kunnen hebben.”
new_statements.translation: p. 90: “2. Word stress as the carrier of the contrast. The contrast is located in the syllable with word stress. Compounds, incidentally, have (at least) two such positions, because each component word independently contributes a word accent. 3. Sentence accents. Independently of the tone contrast, words are accented in the sentence in the same way as in Standard German and Standard Dutch.” p. 105: “Hermans (1994) mentions words with stress on the antepenultimate and secondary stress on the final syllable, such as 1alge1bra, 1domi1nee, which in the Maasbracht dialect can only have Accent 2.”

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's weight-hedged, Dutch-type reading from Gussenhoven 2000 (Roermond) and Peters 2006 (Hasselt): confirms that the tone contrast is anchored to the word-stressed syllable and that sentence accent works as in Standard Dutch, and adds that secondary stress on final syllables exists and can carry Accent 2 (Venlo). It is silent on the placement algorithm itself, which is why the catalog's existing tag for this source ('read: silent on stress') is also defensible; the quotes here match the ones the catalog already holds for it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Limburgish has a binary lexical tone-accent contrast (Accent 1 vs Accent 2) that is confined to the syllable bearing word stress (one locus per simplex word, one per member in compounds); sentence accent is placed as in Standard Dutch/German. The survey presupposes a Dutch-type word-stress system and gives no placement algorithm; it shows that antepenult main stress with final secondary stress occurs (algebra, dominee) and, on p. 106, that in Venlo Accent 2 can also occur on a final syllable with secondary stress (olifant).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Present: words like algebra, dominee carry main stress on the antepenult and secondary stress on the final syllable (Maasbracht, after Hermans 1994, p. 105); in Venlo the tone contrast can appear on a final secondarily-stressed syllable too, so Accent 2 can occur twice in olifant (p. 106).
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress placement; the distributional restrictions discussed (pp. 105-106) concern which stressed rimes can carry the tone contrast (two sonorant moras in East Limburgish; Roermond/Maasbracht restrictions for /in, yn, un/ + nasal and nasal + voiceless obstruent).
new_statements.identity_note: Peters 2008 is about the dialect of Hasselt (Belgian Limburg, West Limburgish). Gussenhoven & Peters 2008 is a survey of the whole Limburgish tone area; its stress remarks are general (p. 90) or cite specific dialects: Maasbracht (Hermans 1994, p. 105) and Venlo (Gussenhoven & van der Vliet 1999, p. 106); it treats Hasselt and Roermond as the two worked grammars (sec. 3). The catalog entry itself covers Roermond (Gussenhoven 2000) and Hasselt (Peters 2006).

new_statements.quote: (p. 983, abstract) "The West-Limburgian dialect of Hasselt has a word accent distinction comparable to the distinction between accent 1 and accent 2 in Swedish and Norwegian. [...] The results suggest that Hasselt speakers, like speakers of the more eastern dialects of Venlo, Roermond, and Cologne, mark accent 2 by lexical tone, while accent 1 remains lexically toneless." (p. 986) "The word accent distinction is confined to word stressed syllables but not to primary word stress. Examples for words with accent 2 in a secondary stressed syllable are /'al2'tet2/ 'always' and /'øø2le'fant2/ 'elephant'. [...] In contrast to East-Limburgian dialects, the Hasselt dialect does not restrict the word accent contrast to syllables containing two or more sonorant moras."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for limb1263 has an empty rule and there are no existing statements. This article adds that the Hasselt dialect is a tone-accent (pitch accent) system in which a lexical tone contrast rides on word-stressed syllables (primary or secondary), with the syllable as TBU; it does not supply a word-stress placement rule, so it neither confirms nor contradicts any placement. Compatible with the companion DBNL text already held by the project (Gussenhoven & Peters 2008, 'Het contrast is gelokaliseerd in de lettergreep met woordklemtoon').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hasselt (West Limburgish) has a privative lexical tone-accent contrast of the Scandinavian accent-1/accent-2 type: accent 2 syllables carry a lexical L tone, accent 1 syllables are lexically toneless; the contrast is licensed only in syllables bearing word stress (primary or secondary) and, unlike Venlo/Roermond/Cologne, is not restricted to syllables with two sonorant moras (CVC syllables can bear accent 2); the TBU is the stressed syllable rather than the sonorant mora; one intonational pitch accent LH* docks on stressed syllables. The article presupposes Germanic-type word stress (marks it with ˈ and ˌ in transcriptions) but nowhere states a rule for where word stress falls.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary word stress exists and can host the tone-accent contrast (accent 2 on secondary-stressed syllables in 'always', 'elephant', p. 986); reduced schwa syllables 'do not count as a bearer of full word stress' (fn. 7, p. 1015). No placement rule for secondary stress is given.
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 5: no basis for distinguishing stressed accent-1 syllables from stressed syllables without accent (accent 1 = default/toneless); East Limburgish (Venlo, Roermond, Cologne) restricts the contrast to stressed syllables with at least two sonorant moras, Hasselt does not (Staelens 1989 vs Grootaers & Grauls 1930 disagree on CVC accent 2; Peters' data support accent 2 on CVC). In accent-2 words the focal peak is displaced to the last syllable before the next stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Peters 2008 describes the West-Limburgian dialect of Hasselt (Belgian Limburg; nine speakers aged 49-82), with systematic comparison to the East-Limburgian dialects of Venlo and Roermond and to Cologne; the catalog entry limb1263 bundles 'Roermond Dutch and the dialect of Hasselt', and the article covers the Hasselt half directly and Roermond only by comparison (Roermond: lexical H on the second sonorant mora of the stressed syllable, contrast restricted to bimoraic stressed syllables).

tone_statements.citation: Ramachers, Stefanie. 2018. Setting the Tone: Acquisition and processing of lexical tone in East-Limburgian dialects of Dutch. PhD dissertation, Radboud Universiteit Nijmegen. Utrecht: LOT (LOT Dissertation Series 485). ISBN 978-94-6093-269-4.
tone_statements.quote: However, the word prosodic contrast in Roermond Dutch is clearly tonal ... There is only a two-way contrast, which has been described as privative. ... the lexical tone system is a crucial element of the Roermond Dutch grammar, since any primary stressed bimoraic syllable (i.e., a syllable consisting of a long vowel, a diphthong, or a short vowel plus a sonorant consonant) carries either accent 1 or accent 2 (Gussenhoven, 2000b). ... The tone bearing unit in Roermond Dutch – the element with which the tone can be associated – is the mora.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 48-49, section 2.2.3 'Word-level pitch in Roermond Dutch' and p. 53, section 2.3
tone_statements.summary: Own terms: 'restricted tone language', privative lexical tone (after Gussenhoven 2000b); contrast only on the primary-stressed bimoraic syllable, one per morpheme; metrical no-tone views cited only.

tone_statements.citation: Goossens, Jan. 2017. De oorsprong van de Rijnlands-Limburgse tweetonigheid: een analyse met bijzondere aandacht voor de korte klinkers voor obstruent. Handelingen van de Koninklijke Commissie voor Toponymie en Dialectologie 89: 129-185.
tone_statements.quote: De Rijnlands-Limburgse tweetonigheid is dus tot stand gekomen doordat hier in een sonoriteitsscala, een gegeven dat in principe in iedere taal van de wereld voorkomt, op een bepaald punt een breuk is ontstaan, die tot een groepering in twee polariserende betoningen heeft geleid.
tone_statements.translation: The Rhenish-Limburgian bitonality thus came about because here, in a sonority scale, something that in principle occurs in every language of the world, a break arose at a certain point, which led to a grouping into two polarising accentuations.
tone_statements.locator: p. 176 (section 5 conclusion); research history pp. 129-140; Haspengouw pp. 148-157
tone_statements.summary: Binary Franconian tone accent (stoottoon/sleeptoon) on stressed syllables incl. short vowel + obstruent rhymes in Genk; partial neutralisation and local loss in Haspengouw/Maastricht area.

tone_statements.citation: Fournier, Rachel & Carlos Gussenhoven. 2012. Measuring phonetic salience and perceptual distinctiveness: the lexical tone contrast of Venlo Dutch. Diadorim: Revista de Estudos Linguísticos e Literários 12. Rio de Janeiro: UFRJ, Programa de Pós-Graduação em Letras Vernáculas. doi:10.35520/diadorim.2012.v12n0a3972 (landing pagehttps://revistas.ufrj.br/index.php/diadorim/article/view/3972)
tone_statements.quote: The shape of the pitch contours in Venlo Dutch (Limburgish) depends not only on which of the two lexical tones occur (Accent 1 or Accent 2), but also on the intonation melody, the presence of an intonational pitch accent and whether the syllable is final or nonfinal in the Intonational Phrase (Gussenhoven & van der Vliet 1999). ... One indication for this is that the contrast between Accent 1 and Accent 2 is lost in nonfocal, nonfinal contexts (Gussenhoven 2000, Fournier, Verhoeven, Swerts and Gussenhoven 2006).
tone_statements.summary: Two lexical tones, Accent 1 vs Accent 2; the source's term is 'lexical tone contrast'; no H/L inventory, TBU or word-stress statement here; contrast neutralized in nonfocal nonfinal syllables.

tone_statements.citation: Hermans, Ben. 2012. The phonological representation of the Limburgian tonal accents. In Bert Botma & Roland Noske (eds.), Phonological Explorations: Empirical, Theoretical and Diachronic Issues, 223-240. Berlin: De Gruyter.
tone_statements.quote: The dialects of Limburg and the adjacent Ripuarian and Moselle Franconian dialects have two tonal accents, Accent 1 and Accent 2. In the generative tradition it is taken for granted that these accents are to be represented tonally. In this article I want to take issue with this approach. ... Specifically, I will argue that Accent 2 is a trochee dominating two syllables, whereas Accent 1 is a monosyllabic trochee. ... My data are taken from the dialect of Maasbracht, in the middle of the Dutch part of Limburg.
tone_statements.summary: Two tonal accents on stressed syllables; author rejects lexical tone (Gussenhoven's H on 2nd mora) for a foot-type analysis. At least 70 accent-marked Maasbracht loans.

tone_statements.citation: Goossens, J. 2011. De Limburgse toonaccenten in het enkelvoud en het meervoud van het woord been. Een oefening in ruimte-tijd-fonologie. Handelingen van de Koninklijke Commissie voor Toponymie en Dialectologie 83: 95-107.
tone_statements.quote: In de heroplevende studie van de Limburgse toonaccenten wordt als kroongetuige van de oppositie tussen sleeptoon en stoottoon telkens opnieuw de tegenstelling tussen het enkelvoud en het meervoud van het woord been genoemd (1). Aangezien het meervoud van dit woord in het Limburgs geen uitgang heeft zou het verschil in toonaccent tussen de sleeptonige enkelvoudsvorm (type bei²n) en de stoottonige meervoudsvorm (type bei¹n) de enige drager van de oppositie zijn. ... In een aantal gevallen is uitsluitend het tooncontrast de drager van de tegenstelling
tone_statements.translation: In the reviving study of the Limburgish tone accents, the contrast between the singular and the plural of the word 'been' (leg/bone) is named again and again as the crown witness of the opposition between sleeptoon (dragging tone) and stoottoon (push tone). Since the plural of this word has no ending in Limburgish, the difference in tone accent between the sleeptoon singular form (type bei²n) and the stoottoon plural form (type bei¹n) would be the sole carrier of the opposition. ... In a number of cases the tone contrast alone is the carrier of the [number] distinction
tone_statements.locator: p. 95, opening paragraph =; last sentence from p. 105
tone_statements.summary: Two tone accents, sleeptoon (²) vs stoottoon (¹), taken as given; dialect-geographic study of one word.

tone_statements.citation: Jongen, R. 2010. De Rijnlandse toonaccenten in het Oost-Nederfrankische dialect van Moresnet. Handelingen van de Koninklijke Commissie voor Toponymie en Dialectologie 82: 37-83.
tone_statements.quote: ...de Ripuarisch-Zuid-N ederfrankische toonaccenten, genaamd stoottoon en sleeptoon, of Schärfung en Trägheitsakzent. ... Het bijzondere kenmerk van de stoottoon/sleeptoon-oppositie is dat ze wel degelijk woordvormdiacritisch fungeert. Daarmee is bedoeld dat de toonaccenten als <<distinctive features>> dienen te worden beschreven, in dezelfde zin als bij voorbeeld <<stemhebbend>> vs. <<stemloos>> bij consonanten, of kort vs. lang bij klinkers. Ze kunnen worden beschouwd als fonologisch-suprasegmentele klinkereigenschappen...
tone_statements.translation: ...the Ripuarian-South Low Franconian tone accents, called stoottoon and sleeptoon, or Schärfung and Trägheitsakzent. ... The special characteristic of the stoottoon/sleeptoon opposition is that it really does function to distinguish word forms. By this is meant that the tone accents must be described as 'distinctive features', in the same sense as e.g. 'voiced' vs 'voiceless' for consonants, or short vs long for vowels. They can be regarded as phonological-suprasegmental vowel properties...
tone_statements.summary: Two-way Rhenish tonal accent (toonaccenten; 'accent tonal.. deux tons') on stressed full vowels, incl. short vowels before obstruents; sleeptoon marks imperative sg; F0 timing per Jongen 1972b.

tone_statements.citation: Verhoeven, Jo. 2007. The Belgian Limburg dialect of Hamont. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 37(2): 219-225. doi:10.1017/S0025100307002940
tone_statements.quote: Traditionally, the Hamont dialect is classified amongst the Limburg dialects with a lexical tone contrast. This lexical tone distinction can signal either lexical differences or grammatical distinctions such as those between the singular and the plural forms of certain nouns. ... In the Hamont dialect, the lexical tone contrast is syllable-based rather than mora-based. ... Since all accented syllables participate in the phonological distinction between Accent 1 and Accent 2, the dialect does not distinguish between Accent 1 and no-Accent.
tone_statements.summary: Two lexical tonal accents (author's term 'lexical tone contrast') on accented syllables incl. monomoraic ones; Accent 1 = fall, Accent 2 = fall-rise (mean F0, 10 speakers); Accent 2 vowels longer.

tone_statements.citation: Fournier, Rachel, Jo Verhoeven, Marc Swerts & Carlos Gussenhoven. 2006. Perceiving word prosodic contrasts as a function of sentence prosody in two Dutch Limburgian dialects. Journal of Phonetics 34(1): 29-48.
tone_statements.quote: In these dialects, number can be marked segmentally or prosodically. The Roermond dialect, but not theWeert dialect, appears to neutralize the prosodic distinction outside the focus constituent in IP-internal syllables. We explain this difference between the dialects on the basis of the specific prosodic marking used, duration in the Weert dialect and F0 in the Roermond dialect.
tone_statements.summary: Roermond: F0-based binary tone accent with positional neutralisation; Weert: durational reflex of the former tone contrast.

tone_statements.citation: Hermans, Ben & Marc van Oostendorp. 1999. Synchrone beperkingen op de Sittardse diftongering. Taal en Tongval 51: 166-186.
tone_statements.quote: This article deals with the interaction between diphtongisation and tone structure in Sittard Dutch. Sittard, like other Limburg Dutch dialects, distinguishes between a so-called dragging (hlh) tone and a falling (hl) tone contour on the syllable that carries primary stress in a word. In Sittard Dutch certain mid vowels get diphthongized in a stressed position.
tone_statements.locator: p. 166, English 'Summary' at the head of the article (DBNL HTML); body statement p. ~174 sec. 3 'Lange middenklinkers die een sleeptoon dragen diftongeren nooit.'
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Binary lexical tone-accent contrast (Accent 1 valtoon HL vs Accent 2 sleeptoon) on the primary-stressed syllable; in Sittard the falling accent triggers diphthongization of long mid vowels.

tone_statements.citation: Heijmans, Linda & Carlos Gussenhoven. 1998. The Dutch dialect of Weert. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 28(1-2): 107-112.
tone_statements.quote: Although Weert is usually included in the Limburgian, Ripuarian, and Mosel-Franconian geographical area with lexical tone ..., and its dialect is described as having a tonal contrast by Verhoeven (1992), and Verhoeven and Connell (1992), it is in fact non-tonal (Heijmans 1999). It has an intonation system which is very similar to that of the standard language. The reason why it has been classified as tonal is probably that well-known tonal minimal pairs in the more easterly dialects, like [bɛin] 'leg' ... vs. [bɛin] 'legs' ... correspond to [bɛin] versus [bæjn] in Weert
tone_statements.summary: Weert stated non-tonal, crediting first author's Heijmans 1999; the 2 pitch-labelled forms ('leg' falling-rising, 'legs' sharply falling) are from eastern tonal dialects, not Weert. IPA from image.

tone_statements.citation: Goossens, J[an]. 1959. Historisch onderzoek van sleeptoon en stoottoon in het dialect van Genk. Handelingen van de Koninklijke Commissie voor Toponymie en Dialectologie 33: 141-212. doi:10.21825/hctd.88161. [Also issued separately, Tongeren: Michiels, 1959, as cited by Gussenhoven & Peters 2008.] Open PDF:https://openjournals.ugent.be/hctd/article/id/88161/download/pdf/
tone_statements.quote: De sleeptonige klank heeft in het Genks van het begin af zijn volle kracht; de intensiteit neemt geleidelijk af en sterft langzaam uit. De klinker maakt op mijn gehoor de indruk dalend te zijn. De stoottonige klank heeft van het begin af zijn volle kracht en behoudt die tot op het einde; dan wordt hij plotseling afgebroken. ... Waar op vele plaatsen de sleeptoon muzikaal stijgend, de stoottoon dalend is, zijn beide accenten dus te Genk muzikaal dalend. ... Toch kunnen de twee accenten nog duidelijk uit elkaar gehouden worden, en door het verschil in lengte, en door de intensiteit
tone_statements.translation: In Genk the dragging-tone (sleeptoon) sound has its full force from the start; the intensity gradually decreases and slowly dies away. To my ear the vowel gives the impression of falling. The push-tone (stoottoon) sound has its full force from the start and keeps it to the end; then it is abruptly broken off. ... Whereas in many places the sleeptoon is musically rising and the stoottoon falling, in Genk both accents are musically falling. ... Yet the two accents can still be clearly kept apart, both by the difference in length and by the intensity
tone_statements.summary: Two-way Rhenish-Limburgian tone accent (sleeptoon ~ Acc. 2, stoottoon ~ Acc. 1); auditory, called provisional; fn. p. 143 previews lab results (sleeptoon mostly rising). Count: floor pp.150-1,201-2.

tone_statements.citation: Goossens, J. 1956. Stoottoon en diftongering van Wgm. î en û in Limburg. Taal en Tongval 8: 99-112.
tone_statements.quote: Er is nog een derde geval: op een aantal plaatsen worden wgm. î en û voor een medeklinker gediftongeerd indien hun reflex stoottonig is (verscherping vertoont).
tone_statements.translation: There is a third case: in a number of places WGmc. long i and long u before a consonant are diphthongised if their reflex carries push tone (shows sharpening).
tone_statements.summary: Binary tone accent presupposed; stoottoon triggers diphthongisation of high long vowels.

tone_statements.citation: Stevens, A. 1955. Intonatieproblemen in en om West-Limburg. Taal en Tongval 7: 135-142.
tone_statements.quote: Een zaak is echter zeker: de fonologische oppositie tussen sleep- en stoottoon is in het betrokken gebied vóór okklusieven en vóór bepaalde kategorieën van spiranten opgeheven wanneer de voorafgaande klank een korte vokaal is.
tone_statements.translation: One thing is certain, however: in the area concerned the phonological opposition between dragging tone and push tone is suspended before occlusives and before certain categories of spirants when the preceding sound is a short vowel.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 141-142 (end of section I.B); also pp. 137-138
tone_statements.summary: Binary tone accent (sleeptoon vs stoottoon), neutralised on short vowel + voiceless obstruent rhymes in East Haspengouw.

tone_statements.citation: Verstegen, V. 1946. Bijdrage tot de tonologie van de Oostlimburgse dialecten. Handelingen van de Koninklijke Commissie voor Toponymie en Dialectologie 20: 99-108.
tone_statements.quote: Voldoende is bekend dat er twee accenten of tonen bestaan die we zullen benoemen met de bij ons best bekende en gemakkelijkste benamingen van sleeptoon en stoottoon. Met een van beide accenten nu wordt elke beklemtoonde lettergreep uitgespröken en die intonatie is dan ook phonologisch relevant. Dit is het geval in onze Zuidnederlandse Limburgse dialecten; mogelijk is dit niet overal zo.
tone_statements.translation: It is sufficiently well known that there are two accents or tones, which we shall call by the names best known and easiest for us, sleeptoon (dragging tone) and stoottoon (push tone). Every stressed syllable is pronounced with one of these two accents, and that intonation is accordingly phonologically relevant. This is the case in our South-Netherlandic Limburgish dialects; possibly it is not so everywhere.
tone_statements.summary: Binary lexical tone accent (sleeptoon/stoottoon) on the stressed syllable, with morphological (number) function and vowel-quality interaction.

tone_statements.citation: Dols, Willy. 1941. Een phonologisch probleem der Limburgsche dialecten. Onze Taaltuin 9: 193-211.
tone_statements.quote: We kunnen nu vragen: heeft in de L.D. èlke beklemtoonde lettergreep een phonologisch relevante intonatie? Het antwoord luidt neen! Want alleen lettergrepen met een langen syllabedrager laten de correlatieve tegenstelling sleeptoon-valtoon toe, lettergrepen met een korten syllabedrager sluiten die uit.
tone_statements.translation: We may now ask: does every stressed syllable in the Limburgish dialects have a phonologically relevant intonation? The answer is no! For only syllables with a long syllable nucleus admit the correlative opposition dragging tone vs falling tone; syllables with a short nucleus exclude it.
tone_statements.summary: Binary lexical tone accent restricted to stressed syllables with two sonorant moras (Sittard).

tone_statements.citation: Kern, J. H. 1909. Zum Verhältnis zwischen Betonung und Laut in niederländisch-limbürgischen Mundarten. Indogermanische Forschungen 26: 258-274.
tone_statements.quote: Expiratorisch sind die Silben in Mstr. entweder eingipflig oder zweigipflig. Unter den ersteren unterscheiden sich solche mit stark geschnittenem Akzent ... von solchen mit schwach geschnittenem ...; musikalisch sind jene eben, diese gleichfalls, oder, namentlich bei sehr nachdrücklicher bezw. stark gedehnter Aussprache, dem Ende zu leise steigend. Die zweigipfligen sind schwach geschnitten und haben musikalisch jäh fallenden Ton: sie springen 'Von einem hochgegriffenen, scheinbar stark hervorgehobenen, schnell verlassenen Anfangstone zu einem tief gelegenen Endtone entschlossen hinab'. Das Intervall ist verschieden, mag aber normal in stark betonter Silbe etwa eine Quart oder Quinte betragen.
tone_statements.translation: In expiratory terms the syllables in Maastricht are either single-peaked or double-peaked. Among the former, those with strongly cut accent ... are distinguished from those with weakly cut accent ...; musically the former are level, the latter likewise, or, especially in very emphatic or strongly lengthened pronunciation, slightly rising towards the end. The double-peaked ones are weakly cut and musically have a sharply falling tone: they jump 'resolutely down from a high-pitched, seemingly strongly emphasised, quickly abandoned initial tone to a low-lying final tone'. The interval varies but may normally amount to about a fourth or a fifth in a strongly stressed syllable.

sources.quote: This article deals with the interaction between diphtongisation and tone structure in Sittard Dutch. Sittard, like other Limburg Dutch dialects, distinguishes between a so-called dragging (hlh) tone and a falling (hl) tone contour on the syllable that carries primary stress in a word. In Sittard Dutch certain mid vowels get diphthongized in a stressed position.

tone.translation: In Genk the dragging-tone (sleeptoon) sound has its full force from the start; the intensity gradually decreases and slowly dies away. To my ear the vowel gives the impression of falling. The push-tone (stoottoon) sound has its full force from the start and keeps it to the end; then it is abruptly broken off. ... Whereas in many places the sleeptoon is musically rising and the stoottoon falling, in Genk both accents are musically falling. ... sources.quote: Expiratorisch sind die Silben in Mstr. entweder eingipflig oder zweigipflig. Die zweigipfligen sind schwach geschnitten und haben musikalisch jäh fallenden Ton: sie springen 'Von einem hochgegriffenen, scheinbar stark hervorgehobenen, schnell verlassenen Anfangstone zu einem tief gelegenen Endtone entschlossen hinab'. Das Intervall ist verschieden, mag aber normal in stark betonter Silbe etwa eine Quart oder Quinte betragen.

tone.translation: In expiratory terms the syllables in Maastricht are either single-peaked or double-peaked. Among the former, those with strongly cut accent ... are distinguished from those with weakly cut accent ...; musically the former are level, the latter likewise, or, especially in very emphatic or strongly lengthened pronunciation, slightly rising towards the end. The double-peaked ones are weakly cut and musically have a sharply falling tone: they jump 'resolutely down from a high-pitched, seemingly strongly emphasised, quickly abandoned initial tone to a low-lying final tone'. The interval varies but may normally amount to about a fourth or a fifth in a strongly stressed syllable.
